phonemes.desc: Aspirated velar /kʰ/ plus short stressed iota — a hard k punched through a puff of breath, pitched high at the acute; the classical chi is an aspirate stop, not yet the modern fricative.
The long diphthong αι, gliding from open a to i — the metrically heavy heart of the name, the syllable Latin later froze into the 'ae' of Chimaera.
Tapped rho plus short open alpha, the feminine ending: the grammar itself insists the monster is a she.

pronunciation.approximation: 'KHEE-mye-rah' — begin with a k followed by a sharp breath, let the middle glide like 'eye', and end on a quick tapped r.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: χίμαρος (chímaros), 'he-goat' — the masculine twin; the monster's name is simply the feminine of the barnyard word, 'she-goat'

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: χεῖμα (kheîma), 'winter, frost' — kin by root: a χίμαιρα is etymologically a 'winterling', a goat one winter old

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: *ǵʰei-, 'snow, winter' (Beekes); cognate with Latin hiems and Sanskrit héman — the fire-breathing monster is built from the word for cold

pronunciation.note: Chímaira is Tier 1 because the Greek Χίμαιρα contains both stress (the acute on the iota) and length (the diphthong αι, metrically long). The restoration preserves both; the ASCII 'chimaira' and the English 'chimera' flatten the accent and melt the diphthong into a bare e.

domains.title: The She-Goat of Fire
domains.subtitle: Fire-Breathing Monster
domains.lead: Chímaira is the monster of Lycia: lion before, serpent behind, she-goat in the middle, breathing forth the dreadful might of blazing fire (Theogony 319–325). Daughter of Typhôn and Echidna, sister to the Hydra and Kerberos, she is Homer's 'thing divine, not of mortal men' — a creature with no cult, no temple, and no pity. And yet her name is the homeliest word in the Greek barnyard: a she-goat one winter old.

cards.name: The Breath of Flame
cards.desc: Her fire is not a weapon she wields but the air she exhales — 'the terrible might of blazing fire' breathed out without cease.

cards.name: The Three-in-One
cards.desc: Lion, goat, and dragon in a single body: the beast that refuses to be one thing, the ancestor of every hybrid the imagination has raised since.

cards.name: The Hero's First Labour
cards.desc: Sent to be killed by her, Bellerophôn instead kills her from the sky — the first monster in Greek myth destroyed from the back of a winged horse.

symbols.name: Flame
symbols.meaning: Her inextinguishable breath of fire — the one feature every source, from Hesiod to Virgil, refuses to omit

symbols.name: Lion forepart
symbols.meaning: The grim-eyed lion's head in front, emblem of her strength and royal ferocity

symbols.name: She-goat's head
symbols.meaning: The goat rising from her middle — the body part that carries her very name, χίμαιρα, 'she-goat'

symbols.name: Serpent tail
symbols.meaning: The dragon (δράκων) behind, her kinship with the earth-born brood of Typhôn made flesh

symbols.name: Pegasos
symbols.meaning: The winged horse, offspring of Poseidôn and Medousa, without whose height no mortal could reach her

symbols.name: Golden bridle of Athēnā
symbols.meaning: The gold-banded bridle the goddess gave Bellerophôn in his dream, the instrument that made the flight — and so the kill — possible

symbols.name: Lead-tipped spear
symbols.meaning: The lump of lead melted by her own swallowed flame, the smith's trick by which Apollodorus says she was burned from within

mythology.lead: Chímaira's myths are all one myth told at different distances: the impossible creature, and the impossible rider sent against her. Born divine, she exists in the tradition only to be destroyed — yet she has never stopped being imagined.

myths.title: Daughter of the Monster-House
myths.text: In the Theogony (319–325), Hesiod sets Chímaira in the brood of Echidna: 'the Chímaira who breathed invincible fire, a creature terrible and great, swift-footed and strong. Three heads she had — one of a fierce-eyed lion, one of a goat, and one of a snake, a mighty dragon: lion in front, dragon behind, goat in the middle — breathing out the dreadful might of blazing fire.' Her siblings are the catalogue of beasts the heroes must undo: Orthos, Kerberos, the Lernaian Hydra. Hesiod seals her fate in the same breath as her birth — 'her did Pegasos and noble Bellerophontês slay' (325) — as if such a creature could only ever be a death postponed.

myths.title: The First Trial of Bellerophôn
myths.text: In Iliad 6 (144–211), Glaukos tells Diomêdês the tale on the battlefield. Spurned by his guest Bellerophôn, Proitos's wife Anteia accused him falsely; unwilling to stain the guest-table with murder, Proitos sent him to Lycia bearing a folded tablet inscribed with 'baneful signs' (σήματα λυγρά, 6.168) — one of the earliest mentions of writing in Greek literature. Reading the letter, the Lycian king set the stranger trials, and first of all bade him slay the Chímaira, the invincible: 'a thing of divine stock, not of men — lion in front, serpent behind, she-goat in the middle, breathing the terrible might of blazing fire' (6.180–182). 'And he slew her, trusting in the portents of the gods' (6.183). The monster meant to be his executioner became the first entry in his glory.

myths.title: Pegasos from the Altar of Athēnā
myths.text: Pindar (Olympian 13.63–92) gives the Corinthian version. The young Bellerophôn longed beyond anything to yoke Pegasos, the winged colt of Medousa, and the seer Polyidos sent him to sleep on Athēnā's altar. In the night the goddess stood beside him and set down a bridle banded with gold, bidding him sacrifice a bull to Poseidôn the Horse-Tamer; he woke with the bridle real in his hands. 'And in bronze armour, mounted upon it, he slew the archer host of the Amazons… and the Chímaira breathing fire' (13.87–90). Pindar grants the beast no anatomy at all — only the flame — and lets the winged horse carry the whole weight of the wonder.

myths.title: Fed with Her Own Fire
myths.text: Apollodorus (Library 2.3.1–2) supplies the mechanism the epics omit. Pegasos, he reminds us, sprang from the severed neck of Medousa, and it was with Athēnā's bridle that Bellerophôn mastered him. Then, mounted, the hero fixed a lump of lead to the point of his spear and flew at the Chímaira; the monster drew the lead down with the fire she breathed, the metal melted in her throat, and her own flame burned out her entrails. The rationalizing detail — a poet's nightmare undone by a smith's trick — is the later age speaking, centuries after Homer, unwilling to let wonder close without an explanation.

lore.syncretism: Rome received her without a cult to domesticate: the Latin Chimaera kept the Greek spelling and lost the goat. Virgil arms her with flame and posts her among the Centaurs and double-formed monsters at the gate of the underworld (Aeneid 6.288), Ovid names her among the hybrid creatures in Byblis's reckoning of unnatural things (Metamorphoses 9.646–648), and Hyginus (Fabulae 57) retells Bellerophôn's hunt for Latin schoolrooms. From there the word drifts from beast to idea: by the Renaissance a 'chimera' is any fire-breathing fancy of the mind, and the she-goat of Lycia has become the common name of impossibility itself.
lore.culturalLegacy: English keeps her twice over. As chimera — and the adjective chimerical — she names the impossible hybrid or the vain, wild fantasy, a sense current in English since the seventeenth century. Science then recruited the monster for real composites: in genetics a chimera is an organism built from two distinct cell lineages, and the ghost-sharks of the deep sea, the family Chimaeridae, bear her name for their mismatched bodies. Every 'chimerical scheme' dismissed in a boardroom is, unknowingly, a Lycian she-goat still breathing fire.
lore.extendedMeditation: The Greeks built her no altar, and yet Homer calls her θεῖον γένος — 'of divine stock, not of men' (Iliad 6.180): the impossible, they felt, deserves a kind of reverence. Commentators have read Hesiod's triple anatomy as a riddle of the Lycian landscape — lion, goat, and serpent as crag, pasture, and fire-vented cleft — but the poet offers no key; the monster simply refuses to be one thing. There is a dry humour buried in the sources: Iliad 16.328 says a man named Amisodaros 'reared' her, as one rears livestock, to be 'a bane to many men' — the Greeks imagined the ungovernable and then gave it a goatherd. The deepest wordplay is the name itself: the most impossible creature in Greek myth carries the tamest noun in the language, a one-winter she-goat; terror, the grammar insists, is bred in the barnyard.
lore.archaeology: She had no sanctuary — monsters seldom do — but her landscape survives: the natural-gas flames of Yanartaş near ancient Phaselis in Lycia have burned without fuel for millennia, and ancient writers from Ctesias to Pliny (Natural History 2.111) knew the undying fire of Mount Chimaera as a landmark for sailors. In art she is among the earliest Greek monsters, attacked by Bellerophôn and Pegasos on Corinthian and Attic vases from the seventh century BC onward, and the Etruscans cast her masterpiece — the bronze Chimaira of Arezzo (c. 400 BC), a lion with the goat's head rising from its back and a serpent for a tail, dedicated to the god Tinia as its inscribed leg (tinścvil) records. Pausanias (2.4.1) still points out the spring Peirene at Corinth, where Bellerophôn was said to have seized the winged horse for the hunt.
